nameStory: The "clasping" in this plant's name comes from how its leaves wrap around and clasp the stem without a leaf stalk - they literally embrace the plant like a hug! Water horehound gets its name from its love of wet places and its membership in the mint family, though it's quite different from the European herb called horehound that was used in old cough remedies.
description: Clasping water horehound is a modest wetland plant in the mint family that grows 1-3 feet tall in wet soils. Unlike showier mints, this one produces tiny white flowers clustered where the leaves meet the square stem. It has a somewhat weedy appearance with opposite leaves that clasp directly onto the stem without stalks. Despite being in the mint family, it lacks the strong fragrance of its more famous cousins.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite leaves that clasp or wrap around the square stem with no leaf stalk - they attach directly to the stem like they're giving it a hug. The leaves are toothed along the edges and feel somewhat rough to the touch.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers clustered in dense whorls where the leaves meet the stem, almost hidden among the foliage. Each flower is barely 1/8 inch across and easy to miss unless you look closely.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows 1-3 feet tall in clumps, with the characteristic square stems of the mint family that you can feel by rolling the stem between your fingers.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, hard nutlets that develop where the flowers were, typically four per flower cluster, feeling like tiny pebbles when mature.

habitat: Look for clasping water horehound in wet meadows, stream banks, pond edges, and marshy areas throughout New England. It thrives in consistently moist to wet soils and can tolerate some flooding. You'll often find it growing alongside other wetland plants like sedges, rushes, and other water-loving mints.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from the wet soil, showing the characteristic clasping leaves early in the season.
seasonality.summer: Blooms from mid to late summer with tiny white flower clusters. This is the best time for identification when both flowers and the distinctive clasping leaves are visible.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and small seed nutlets develop. Leaves may begin to yellow but the plant structure remains identifiable.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to the ground, leaving only underground parts to survive the cold season.

funFact: Despite being in the mint family, clasping water horehound was traditionally used by some Native American tribes as a natural insect repellent - quite the opposite effect of most fragrant mints that tend to attract pollinators and other insects!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other water horehounds in the same genus, but the clasping leaves (no leaf stalks) are the key difference - other bugleweed species have leaves with distinct stalks. Memory trick: "Clasping water horehound clasps the stem!"
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this "horehound" with the European white horehound (Marrubium vulgare) used in cough drops and traditional medicine - they're different plants entirely. The water horehounds got their name simply from being mint family plants found in wet places, not from any medicinal similarity.
compareHints: Among its water horehound relatives, clasping water horehound is unique for its sessile leaves (botanist speak for "no leaf stalk") that wrap around the stem. Northern bugleweed and American bugleweed both have leaves with distinct stalks, while European water horehound has more deeply cut, almost lacy-looking leaves. The clasping leaf feature makes this species relatively easy to distinguish once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the water horehounds, northern bugleweed is the shortest and most delicate, typically staying under 20 inches tall compared to American bugleweed which can reach 4 feet.
Among the water horehounds in New England, American bugleweed is typically the most robust and tall-growing species.
Among New England's water horehounds, sweet bugleweed stands out for its pleasant mint fragrance and hidden stamens.
Compared to native bugleweeds like American bugleweed, European water-horehound tends to have more coarsely toothed leaves and slightly showier flower clusters.
Among New England's water horehounds, taperleaf is distinguished by its notably narrow, lance-shaped leaves that taper dramatically to sharp points.
